Planting garlic in the autumn rain
Posted in Vegetables
Every October I plant garlic, and every October it rains. This year was no different, and I spent a soggy afternoon on my knees in the bed by the shed.
Garlic needs a cold spell to split into cloves. If you plant it in spring, you often get a single round bulb instead. That is still edible, but it is not what most of us are hoping for.
I push each clove about five centimetres deep, pointed end up, with a hand span between them. Then I cover the bed with a thin layer of compost and forget about it until March.
By midsummer the leaves start to yellow from the tips. That is the signal to lift the bulbs and hang them somewhere dry and airy for a few weeks.
